vignette:
Marcus

Marcus sits in the leather chair across from me with his shoulders drawn inward, a posture that seems to have become permanent. At fifty-eight, he carries himself like someone much older—not from the weight of years, but from the weight of something else entirely. His wife, Priya, sits beside him today. She reaches for his hand occasionally, a gesture that seems more about reassurance for herself than for him. He doesn't pull away, but he doesn't squeeze back either.

Twenty-three months ago, Marcus was on a business trip to oversee a product launch in Lahore. He'd been a product manager for a tech company for nearly two decades, comfortable in his role, respected by his teams. The trip was routine—meetings, presentations, the kind of work travel he'd done hundreds of times. But on the third evening, after leaving a client dinner, he took a wrong turn in an unfamiliar neighborhood. Within minutes, three men pulled him into an alley.

What happened over the next four hours exists in his memory like a film with missing frames. He knows he was beaten. He knows they demanded money, then demanded information about his company, then seemed to want nothing except to inflict pain. He remembers a metal pipe. He remembers his own voice breaking as he begged them to stop. He remembers the smell of his own blood and urine. The rest comes to him in fragments—sensations without sequence, terror without narrative.

The police found him unconscious. He was hospitalized for two weeks with three broken ribs, a fractured wrist, and a concussion. The physical injuries healed. The rest of him did not.

Now, sitting in my office, Marcus describes his days with the flatness of someone recounting a grocery list. He returns to work last month—a decision he made against Priya's wishes. Product management requires strategic thinking, collaboration, presence. Marcus finds himself unable to do any of it. In meetings, he feels hypervigilant, certain that the casual proximity of colleagues poses a threat. When his boss approached him from behind to review something on his screen, Marcus flinched so violently he knocked over his coffee. The embarrassment burned deeper than the fear.

He doesn't sleep more than three or four hours a night. When he does sleep, he wakes gasping, his body drenched in sweat, convinced he's back in that alley. Priya lies awake beside him now, listening to his breathing, waiting for the nightmares. He's stopped attending the weekly dinner gatherings with friends. He avoids restaurants. He won't travel, even for work, which has created tension with his company.

What troubles him most, he tells me, is the anger. Marcus has always been a measured man—thoughtful, diplomatic. Now he finds himself furious at small things. A delayed email. Traffic. The sound of Priya's alarm in the morning. He snaps at her, then feels immediate remorse that somehow makes it worse. He's angry at himself for being weak, for being afraid of shadows, for not fighting back harder in that alley. He's angry at the men, at the city, at God or whatever was supposed to protect him.

He's stopped eating the South Asian food Priya cooks, though he can't quite explain why. He avoids the news. He checks the locks on the doors multiple times before bed. When he does venture outside, he maps exits and stays alert to everyone around him. Part of him knows this hypervigilance isn't rational, but knowing doesn't change anything. His body refuses to believe he's safe.

Marcus looks at his hands as he talks. Priya looks at him with an expression that mingles love with something else—exhaustion, maybe, or grief for the husband she had before.
